# Concept: Resampling to Estimate Test Error

## Why resampling?

We established that training error is optimistic. A single train/test split gives an unbiased but noisy estimate. **Resampling methods** use the available data more efficiently by repeatedly fitting models on subsets and averaging the results.

## Three approaches

| Method | Idea | Bias | Variance | Use when |
|--------|------|------|----------|----------|
| **Validation set** | Single 70/30 split | Low | High | Very large n |
| **k-fold CV** | Rotate through k folds | Moderate | Moderate | Standard choice |
| **LOOCV** | k = n | Very low | High | Small n, cheap models |
| **Bootstrap** | Sample with replacement | Low | Low | Also estimates parameter uncertainty |

## k-fold cross-validation

1. Randomly divide data into $k$ equal folds
2. For $j = 1, \ldots, k$: fit model on all folds except $j$, predict on fold $j$
3. Average the $k$ test errors: $\text{CV}_{(k)} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^k \text{MSE}_j$

Typical choices: $k=5$ or $k=10$. These balance bias (LOOCV has lowest) and variance (smaller $k$ has lower variance because training sets are less similar).

## The bootstrap

Draw $B$ samples of size $n$ **with replacement** from the training data. Fit the model on each bootstrap sample, evaluate on the original data (out-of-bag observations). Useful for estimating both test error and parameter uncertainty.

# Quiz

```{=html}
<div class="sta240-quiz" data-question="In 5-fold cross-validation on n=100 observations, how many observations are in each test fold?">
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="false">5</div>
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="true">20</div>
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="false">80</div>
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="false">100</div>
  <div class="q-exp">n/k = 100/5 = 20 observations per test fold. Each fold is used exactly once as the test set. The model is trained on the remaining 80 observations and evaluated on the 20 held-out ones.</div>
</div>

<div class="sta240-quiz" data-question="LOOCV has lower bias but higher variance than 10-fold CV. Why?">
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="false">LOOCV uses less data for training than 10-fold CV</div>
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="true">The n LOOCV training sets overlap almost completely, making the n MSE estimates highly correlated</div>
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="false">LOOCV averages over fewer folds so the mean is less stable</div>
  <div class="q-opt" data-correct="false">LOOCV gives biased estimates for nonlinear models</div>
  <div class="q-exp">In LOOCV, each training set of size n−1 differs from the others by just one observation. This means the n model fits (and their errors) are nearly identical — highly correlated. Averaging correlated estimates barely reduces variance. In 10-fold CV the 10 test sets are more distinct, giving less correlated estimates and lower variance of the CV estimate.</div>
</div>
```

# Worked Example

```{r}
#| label: cv-demo
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
f_true <- function(x) sin(pi * x)
n <- 80
x <- sort(runif(n, 0, 1))
y <- f_true(x) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)

# Manual 10-fold CV
k <- 10
folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out=n))
degrees <- 1:10

cv_mse <- sapply(degrees, function(d) {
  fold_errs <- sapply(1:k, function(j) {
    tr <- which(folds != j)
    te <- which(folds == j)
    fit <- lm(y[tr] ~ poly(x[tr], d))
    xp  <- poly(x[te], d, coefs=attr(poly(x[tr], d), "coefs"))
    mean((y[te] - cbind(1, xp) %*% coef(fit))^2)
  })
  mean(fold_errs)
})

res <- data.frame(degree=degrees, cv_mse=cv_mse,
                  train_mse=sapply(degrees, function(d)
                    mean(residuals(lm(y ~ poly(x, d)))^2)))

ggplot(res, aes(x=degree)) +
  geom_line(aes(y=train_mse), colour="#2980b9", linewidth=1.2) +
  geom_line(aes(y=cv_mse),   colour="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y=cv_mse), colour="#e74c3c", size=2.5) +
  geom_vline(xintercept=degrees[which.min(cv_mse)],
             linetype="dashed", colour="#27ae60") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=degrees) +
  labs(title="10-fold CV vs training error",
       subtitle=paste0("Green dashed = optimal degree by CV (", degrees[which.min(cv_mse)], ")  |  Red = CV MSE  |  Blue = Training MSE"),
       x="Degree", y="MSE") +
  theme_minimal()
```

# Guided Practice

::: {.webr-loading-note}
**R is loading** — exercises interactive once ready.
:::

```{webr-r}
#| label: guided-cv
set.seed(42)
f_true <- function(x) sin(pi * x)
n <- 80
x <- sort(runif(n, 0, 1))
y <- f_true(x) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.4)

# TASK 1: Implement 5-fold CV for degrees 1:10
k <- 5
folds <- sample(rep(1:k, length.out=n))
degrees <- 1:10

cv5 <- sapply(degrees, function(d) {
  mean(sapply(1:k, function(j) {
    tr <- which(folds != j); te <- which(folds == j)
    fit <- lm(y[tr] ~ poly(x[tr], d))
    xp  <- poly(x[te], d, coefs=attr(poly(x[tr], d), "coefs"))
    mean((y[te] - cbind(1, xp) %*% coef(fit))^2)
  }))
})

cat("5-fold CV MSE by degree:\n")
for (i in seq_along(degrees)) {
  cat(sprintf("  Degree %2d: %.4f\n", degrees[i], cv5[i]))
}
cat("\nOptimal degree:", degrees[which.min(cv5)], "\n")

# TASK 2: Compare 5-fold and 10-fold CV results
# (repeat above with k=10 and compare which degree they select)
```
